statement: Lecture 5 agenda: relational databases and pessimistic locking; designing an airline check-in system; designing a key-value store on a relational database.
detail: Title slide reads `SYSTEM DESIGN MASTERCLASS Databases`.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Agenda: - Relational Databases & Pessimistic locking - Designing: Airline Checkin System - Designing: KV Store on relational DB

statement: In a relational database, data is stored and represented in rows and columns.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Data is stored & represented in rows and column

statement: The key highlight of relational databases is relations: you pick a relational database for relations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Key highlight of relational database are Relations ... You pick relational databases for relations.

statement: Relational databases are known for ACID guarantees; ACID itself is covered in the pre-reads.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Relational Databases are known for ACID * Refer to pre-reads for understanding ACID

statement: Database indexes make reads faster and writes slower.
detail: Board refers to the teacher's YouTube video 'How indexes make DB read faster?'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Indexes make reads faster and writes slower

statement: Pessimistic locking (database locking): the core idea is that you acquire the lock before proceeding.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Database Locking : [ Pessimistic Locking ] Core idea: You acquire the lock before proceeding

statement: Typical pessimistic-locking flow: acquire the lock, read/update (the critical section), release the lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Typical Flow → ACQ_LOCK() READ UPDATE REL_LOCK()

statement: There are two types of (pessimistic) locking strategies: shared locks and exclusive locks.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Two types of locking strategies - Shared lock - Exclusive lock

statement: Locks are needed to protect the sanity of the data (its consistency and integrity), i.e. to protect data against concurrent updates.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why do we need locks To protect the sanity of the data ... Consistency Integrity Protecting the data against concurrent updates

statement: The risk that comes with pessimistic locking is a transactional deadlock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Risk: Transactional Deadlock !!

statement: When a deadlock would occur, the transaction that detects the deadlock kills itself.
detail: Diagram D-01: T1 → Row 1 and Row 2 → T1, with the other half of the cycle (T2) hidden behind the participant tiles.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The transaction that detects the deadlock kills itself !

statement: Shared lock: rows are reserved for read by the current transaction; other transactions can read the locked rows but cannot modify them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: reserved for read by the current transaction - other transactions can read the locked rows - other transactions cannot modify the locked rows

statement: If the transaction holding a shared lock wants to modify the rows, its lock is upgraded to an exclusive lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if the current transaction wants to modify then the locks will be upgraded to an exclusive lock

statement: A shared lock is taken by ending a SELECT with FOR SHARE.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SELECT * FROM ....... FOR SHARE;

statement: FOR SHARE example: Transaction 1 locks user_id IN (1,2,6) and can read and modify; Transaction 2 locks user_id IN (3,4,6) and can read but must wait to modify because row 6 is shared.
detail: Labels `READ & MO` / `READ & WAI` are cut off at the tile column; full `READ & MODIFY` is visible at 00:19:18. Diagram D-02.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Transaction 1 READ & MO.. WHERE user_id IN (1,2,6) FOR SHARE; Transaction 2 READ & WAI.. WHERE user_id IN (3,4,6) FOR SHARE

statement: Exclusive lock: rows are reserved for write by the current transaction; other transactions can neither read nor modify the locked rows.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: reserved for write by the current transaction - other transactions cannot read the locked rows - other transactions cannot modify the locked rows

statement: An exclusive lock is taken by ending a SELECT with FOR UPDATE.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SELECT * FROM ....... FOR UPDATE;

statement: FOR UPDATE example: Transaction 1 locks user_id IN (1,2,6); Transaction 2 asking for user_id IN (3,4,6) has to wait because row 6 is exclusively locked.
detail: Diagram D-03; red emphasis at 00:22:45 on the overlapping row 6.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Transaction 1 READ & MO.. WHERE user_id IN (1,2,6) FOR UPDATE ; Transaction 2 WAIT WHERE user_id IN (3,4,6) FOR UPDATE ;

statement: SKIP LOCKED removes the locked rows from the result set: if a row is locked, the query skips it instead of waiting.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SKIP LOCKED Removes the locked rows from the result set ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; if the row is locked it would skip it

statement: NOWAIT: a locking read does not wait for the lock to be acquired; it fails immediately if the row is locked (the transaction is killed).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: NOWAIT locking read does not wait for the lock to be acquired. It fails immediately ... if the row is locked kill the transaction

statement: In MySQL, a NOWAIT read on a locked row fails with error 3572 (do not wait for lock).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT ; ERROR 3572 : DO NOT WAIT FOR LOCK

statement: Airline check-in system requirements: multiple airlines, each airline has multiple planes (flights), each flight has 120 seats, each flight has multiple trips, and a user books a seat in one trip of a flight.

verbatim: - Multiple airlines - Every airline has multiple plane (flight) - Each flight has 120 seats - Every flight has multiple trips ...

detail: Restated at 00:29:24: `How will we handle when all 120 people flying in one flight in the same trip check-in at the same time!`
case_study: Airline check-in system demo (120 seats per flight, many users checking in at once).
speaker: teacher

statement: Approach 2: all users book random seats concurrently with no checks (last one wins); several users end up 'booking' the same seat and far fewer seats are actually filled.

statement: Approach 4: select the first available seat and lock it exclusively with FOR UPDATE; all 120 users get distinct seats, filled in order, in about 1.2-1.8 s.

statement: Approach 5: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; all 120 seats are still filled correctly but the run takes about 147 ms instead of over a second.

verbatim: ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED ... took 147.4798ms

statement: Second design problem: a distributed key-value store on a relational database (Apache Ignite is the reference); requirements are infinite scalability and GET, PUT, DEL and TTL.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Distributed KV store on relational database Requirements: - Infinitely Scalable - GET, PUT, DEL, TTL Apache Ignite

statement: The KV-store brainstorm covers storage, optimizing storage, insert, update and TTL; TTL is key-specific.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Brainstorm : Storage , optimize storage , Insert , Update, TTL ... Keyspecific

statement: Store table schema: key as the primary key with a fixed-size type such as varchar(16), and value as a BLOB.
detail: `varchra` [sic, varchar]. Audio says the key size must be fixed up front (16, 24, ...).
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: store key PK ( varchra (16) ) value (BLOB)

statement: Proposed TTL columns created_at and ttl_sec, with a cleanup query deleting rows where now() - created_at exceeds the TTL.
detail: Teacher's correction: this query cannot use an index (dynamic computation), so it scans every row; store an absolute expired_at instead.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: key value created_at ttl_sec ... Delete store where now() - create..

statement: Store an absolute expiry time (expired_at) instead of created_at + TTL, so the cleanup is an indexable query: delete from store where expired_at <= now().
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: expired_at ... Delete store where expired_at <= now ... BG Job Delete from store where expired_at <= now();

statement: Delete is a soft delete: update store set expired_at = -1 where key = k; the background job then hard-deletes it with the expired keys.
detail: An is_del = True column with its own BG job was written first (01:46:30) and erased by 01:50; -1 in expired_at replaces it.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Soft delete update str set expired_at = ... Delete ↳ update store set exp_at = -1 where key = k

statement: Insert is insert into store values (k, v, e); two PUTs on the same key (Put k1 v1, Put k1 v2) make the second insert fail because key is the primary key.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Insert ↳ insert into store values (k, v, e); Put k₁ v₁ Put k₁ v₂ ... key → PK

statement: PUT is implemented as an UPSERT (MySQL: REPLACE INTO or INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE) instead of a GET followed by INSERT/UPDATE.
detail: Prepared notes (02:04:45): `key exist → update`, `key does not exist → insert`, `REPLACE INTO 'store' VALUES ( k, v, ttl )` for MySQL, `postgreSQL → UPSERT statement`.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: UPSERT ... upsert into store values (k, v₂, e); " Replace into " " ON Duplicate Key Update "

statement: GET must hide expired keys: select * from store where key = k and expired_at > now().
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: GET Select * from store where key = k, and expired_at > now()

statement: Storage: use MySQL, start with a single node and then scale as the system demands.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Storage: MySQL start with single node & then scale as the system demands

statement: Final schema notes: key and value; ttl as an absolute expiration time; is_deleted for soft delete. To save storage, drop is_deleted and use ttl = -1 as the special value marking deletion.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Saving storage: why have another column for is_deleted ? ... ttl → -1 special value marking deletion

statement: Hard delete is a batch, periodic cleanup: a separate process hard-deletes the soft-deleted rows, which minimizes I/O and rebalancing.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: How to hard delete? Batch & periodic cleanup - Run a separate cleanup process to hard delete the soft deleted rows ... minimize I/O

statement: Multiple concurrent PUTs on a key are handled with locks (protecting data integrity): when one is updating, the other waits, e.g. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT then UPDATE store SET value = v2 WHERE key = k1.
detail: Board pairs 'other waits' with a NO WAIT example; as written.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Multiple PUT requests? locks → protects data integrity ... when one is updating other waits ... FOR UPDATE NO WAIT ;

statement: TTL approach 1: batch deletion with a CRON job that hard-deletes every t minutes; expired keys not yet deleted are filtered out on read (where key = k and ttl > now()).
detail: Diagram D-07.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Approach 1: Batch deletion with CRON Job ... t minutes Hard delete ... What about expired keys before they are hard delet.. - filter out

statement: TTL approach 2: lazy deletion (in-memory) - hard-delete an expired key when it is fetched; a key that is never fetched is never deleted, so a CRON job is still needed.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Lazy deletion [in-mem] Do hard delete when an expired key is fetched * what if the key is never fetched ?

statement: TTL approach 3 (random sampling and deletion, not suitable for disk-backed DBs): randomly sample 20 keys that have expiration set, delete the expired ones, and repeat if more than 25% were deleted.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Approach 3 : Random Sampling & Deletion * Not suitable for disk backed DBs - Randomly sample 20 keys having expiration set ...

statement: Idea behind sampling: if a sample has under 25% expired keys, the population will have under 25% expired (not yet deleted) keys.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Idea: if sample has < 25% of expired keys , population will have < 25% of expired keys (not deleted)

statement: Redis uses the random-sampling expiry approach, and the sample size of 20 comes from the Central Limit Theorem.
detail: Recorded as written; to be fact-checked.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: * This approach is used by Redis & the number ( sample size ) 20 comes from the Central limit Theorem

statement: Implementing delete: UPDATE store SET ttl = -1 WHERE key = k1 AND ttl > NOW(); the ttl > NOW() condition avoids rewriting already-expired rows, reducing the load on disk.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: UPDATE store SET ttl = -1 WHERE key = k₁ AND ttl > NOW(); reducing the load on disk

statement: Implementing batch cleanup: DELETE FROM store WHERE ttl <= now() removes both expired and soft-deleted keys.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: DELETE FROM store WHERE ttl <= now(); expired and soft deleted

statement: KV store high-level architecture: users → load balancer → many stateless KV-API servers → MySQL, with a periodic batch-cleanup job on MySQL; add as many KV-API servers as the load needs, assuming MySQL handles the incoming load.
detail: Diagram D-08.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: High level Architecture ... * We add as many KV API servers to support the load ... assuming MySQL is handling the incoming load

statement: If reads dominate (99:1) and one DB cannot handle them, add read replicas - but only when reading stale data is okay.
detail: Diagram D-09.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If we have a 99:1 read requests and one DB is not able to handle it, we add read replicas ... stale data is okay

statement: If the master sees a lot of writes, first scale it up vertically; if it still cannot handle the load, partition.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If Master is now seeing a lot of writes - we first vertically scale-up - if it is still not able ... we partition

statement: Partitioned KV store: keys are split by range across masters (Master 1 [a-m], Master 2 [n-z]), each with its own replica and batch-cleanup job; every KV-API connects to all masters, and each master owns an exclusive fragment of the data.
detail: Diagram D-10.
case_study: Distributed key-value store built on a relational database (MySQL).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Master 1 [a-m] Master 2 [n-z] ... Each Master node owns an exclusive fragment of the data
